newsitem.title: BRAZIL: After model's coma, Brazil debates plastic surgery.
newsitem.headline: After model's coma, Brazil debates plastic surgery.

text.p: A top model's dangerous coma after plastic surgery last week has ignited a debate about the obsession with beauty that has driven a quarter of a million Brazilians each year to seek cosmetic surgery.

Doctors on Tuesday said fashion model Claudia Liz was recovering well after waking from a four-day coma triggered by an allergic reaction to the anaesthetic she received before liposuction surgery last week.
But they said the six foot (180 cm) blonde was lucky to have avoided brain damage during the operation that took place in a fashionable but ill-equipped Sao Paulo clinic.

Now friends, family and the media are asking whether the successful, 27 year-old woman should have sought painful surgery to lose just four pounds (two kilos) of fat on her thighs to restore her career. Newspapers had reported that Liz, one of Brazil's best-paid models, had been banished from the catwalks until she lost the weight gained over the past few months.

"I didn't want it, the family didn't want it and even Claudia felt she didn't need the liposuction," Liz's husband, Celso Loducca, told reporters at the hospital. "She was two kilos overweight. She was pressured by the market to undergo the operation," a teary Loducca said.

Plastic surgery is a booming industry, with more than 250,000 Brazilians a year seeking a surgical remake, a figure surpassed only by the United States. Nose jobs, face lifts and silicone implants are as routine among the country's prosperous middle-class as root canal surgery.

Parents commonly pay for breast reduction or expansion surgery for their teenage daughters as Christmas or birthday gifts. Actors, models and politicians have confessed to going under the knife, and few people have any inhibitions about saying what part of their body required an overhaul.
Before-and-after newspaper pictures show even President Fernando Henrique Cardoso appears to have had surgery to hide the sagging flesh underneath his eyes.

"This is a hot country where for eight months of the year people spend an awful lot of time either at the beach or by the pool," said Rolf Gemperli, vice president of Brazil's Plastic Surgeon's Association. "When you're showing so much naked skin you can't really afford not to look good."

But Gemperli said cosmetic surgery was not to blame for Liz's life-threatening situation. "Claudia Liz went into a coma not because of liposuction therapy but because of an anaesthetist's inexperience," he said.

Patients who have undergone successful cosmetic surgery argue that people have every right to invest in their bodies and improve their looks. "Good-looking people are better accepted by society, have more attractive job offers and enjoy higher self esteem," said fashion model Luiza Brunet who recently appeared in a glossy personality magazine with refurbished breasts.

With the latest news reports saying Liz may leave the hospital as soon as this weekend, the controvery surrounding plastic surgery will probably die down. The reports said the model was in high spirits and had lost the unwanted weight during her stay in the hospital.
